newsitem.title: IRAQ: UN's Ekeus in Iraq for fresh arms talks.
newsitem.headline: UN's Ekeus in Iraq for fresh arms talks.

text.p: United Nations arms envoy Rolf Ekeus arrived in Baghdad on Thursday to try again to persuade Iraqi leaders to allow removal of wrecked missile engines for analysis in the United Sates, a U.N. source said on Thursday.
The source said the talks, scheduled to last until Sunday, would also touch on Iraq's banned chemical weapons programmes. Ekeus was accompanied by experts in missiles and chemical weapons.

Ekeus heads the U.N. Special Commission disarming Iraq under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms. It must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited oil exports under a humanitarian deal.
Ekeus, a former Swedish diplomat who says Baghdad is still not cooperating fully, came under a scathing attack this week in Babel, the newspaper run by President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday.

"A team of 10 international experts on ballistic missiles and chemical arms accompanies the chairman," the U.N. source said. They included Russian missile expert and veteran arms inspector Nikita Smidovich.
"A meeting with the Iraqi side including Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz is scheduled later today," the source said.
Iraq is carrying out excavations under U.N. supervision in an attempt to prove it has destroyed long-range missiles that Ekeus believes Baghdad has hidden in violation of the ceasefire.
The U.N. source said the Iraqis uncovered another missile component this week in addition to four wrecked engines found last month.

About 100 missile engines have been dug up but Ekeus says he wants the parts examined in the United States to prove they came from the Scuds Baghdad bought from the former Soviet Union before its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

He says engines found so far could have been made in Iraq while the original ones remain hidden. Iraq, accusing Ekeus of seeking to prolong sanctions, rejects the charge and has agreed to have them analysed in France or Russia.
U.N. resolutions do not allow Iraq to have or manufacture missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).
